analysis.investment_thesis: EPW India trades at ~118 INR against a Graham Number of ~19 INR (6x overvalued), with a Price-to-Book of ~25x on a razor-thin equity base of INR 5 Cr. Despite reporting INR 4 Cr net profit, operating cash flow was -11 Cr in FY25 — a fundamental breakdown in earnings quality that disqualifies this stock entirely.
key_strengths: Revenue growing rapidly: 7 → 19 → 53 Cr in three years, demonstrating some commercial traction.
Minimal finance costs (near zero) until FY25 when borrowings jumped to INR 12 Cr.
High promoter holding at 71.43% signals owner-operator alignment.
key_risks: Severe earnings quality failure: INR 4 Cr reported profit vs. -11 Cr operating cash flow — profit is not translating to cash.
Debt-to-Equity of 2.4x (INR 12 Cr borrowings vs. INR 5 Cr equity) — far exceeds my 0.5x limit.
Commoditised refurbished hardware business with no durable competitive moat, operating in a race-to-the-bottom pricing environment.
red_flags: Price-to-Book of ~25.8x — I require <1.5x; this is 17x beyond my ceiling.
Graham Number: ~INR 19 vs. market price of INR 118 — stock is trading at a 6x premium to intrinsic asset-earning value.
Free Cash Flow of -12 Cr in FY25 — the business is consuming, not generating, capital.
Earnings history of just 3 years, with FY23 showing essentially zero profit — fails my 5-year positive earnings requirement.
Micro-cap (INR 129 Cr) with virtually no book value — one bad quarter could wipe equity entirely.
analysis.detailed_analysis:
EPW India fails nearly every quantitative filter I have established over decades of security analysis. The Graham Number — computed as √(22.5 × EPS of ~3.67 × Book Value per share of ~4.58) — yields approximately INR 19, against a market price of INR 118. This means Mr. Market is pricing this company at over six times what arithmetic prudence permits. The P/B of roughly 26x is the most damning single number: investors are paying INR 26 for every rupee of net assets in a commoditised refurbishing business with no proprietary technology, no patents, and no switching costs. The ROE of 139% is a statistical artifact of near-zero equity, not a sign of a durable franchise.

The cash flow statement reveals the deeper problem. A business reporting INR 4 Cr in net profit while burning INR 11 Cr in operating cash flow is either aggressively booking receivables or suffering from working capital deterioration — neither is acceptable. The sudden jump in borrowings from zero to INR 12 Cr in FY25, coinciding with negative free cash flow of -12 Cr, tells me the growth is being funded by creditors, not earned organically. This is precisely the type of speculative, asset-light-in-name-only operation that the intelligent investor must shun. At INR 129 Cr market cap on INR 53 Cr of revenue and INR 5 Cr of equity, there is no margin of safety whatsoever.
